analysis.one_liner: Lets Congress repeal many end-of-term federal regulations with a single vote.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee reported the bill without amendment and placed it on the Senate calendar in September 2026; no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Congress can strike a regulation a departing president's administration issued at the end of its term, but each repeal vote covers only one rule. This bill would let Congress bundle many such "midnight rules" into a single joint resolution of disapproval, so one vote could wipe out dozens of end-of-term regulations at once. It passed through the Senate Homeland Security committee in 2026 and is waiting on the Senate calendar for floor time.
analysis.who_benefits: A congressional majority that wants to strike a departing administration's late-term regulations: they could do it in one vote instead of one vote per rule. Industries that opposed those regulations also benefit, because the rules they faced would be easier to repeal in bulk.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Congressional Review Act so a single joint resolution can disapprove multiple regulations, as long as each was submitted for review during the final year of a president's term.
Under current law each disapproval resolution may target only one regulation, so repealing many rules takes many separate votes; the bill removes that one-at-a-time limit.

analysis.who_pays: Whoever relied on the protections in the struck rules. End-of-term rules often cover environmental, health, safety, and consumer matters, so the people protected by them would lose those protections if Congress voted the bundle down.

drawbacks.text: Bulk repeal would let Congress erase many rules in one vote without debating each one on its merits, including rules that protect public health, safety, or the environment.
The tool cuts both ways: whichever party controls Congress after a presidential transition can use it, so protections many people count on could be struck by a single vote with no individual review.
Supporters argue the change restores accountability for a rush of end-of-term rulemaking and speeds up review; the honest cost is that speed comes at the expense of rule-by-rule scrutiny.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Congress, the bill is a genuine efficiency: what used to take dozens of votes takes one. For the public, the effect depends entirely on which rules get bundled and struck. Some end-of-term rules are genuinely rushed or burdensome; others are significant protections issued late on purpose. Because a bundled vote strips away the individual scrutiny each rule now gets, the public trade is speed and convenience in Washington against the risk of losing specific protections wholesale.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Homeland Security committee reported the bill favorably without amendment in September 2026, and it now sits on the Senate's legislative calendar waiting for floor time; no vote has been taken.

narrative.text: Introduced January 21, 2025 by Sen. Ron Johnson with six Republican cosponsors, and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on August 6, 2026, and it was formally reported by Sen. Paul on September 14, 2026.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 564, meaning it is eligible for floor consideration but has not been brought up for a vote.
No chamber has voted on the bill, and no opposition is recorded in the congressional action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has won or lost yet. The bill is one step from floor consideration; if it stalls on the calendar, the existing one-rule-per-vote process stays in place, which preserves individual scrutiny of each repeal but preserves nothing else in particular.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet — awaiting a floor vote

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans have sponsored or cosponsored the bill so far, but no vote has been taken, so there is no record of how the parties split.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (finance, energy, environmental, and others facing end-of-term rules)
industries.note: The bill makes it far cheaper, politically, to repeal rules those industries opposed: one vote can strike many at once. When the struck rules protect public health, safety, or consumers, the industry's gain is the public's loss.

industries.industry: Public interest, environmental, and consumer groups defending late-term regulations
industries.note: Bundled disapproval removes the rule-by-rule debate these groups rely on to make the case for each protection individually.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee and sits on the Senate calendar, one step from a floor vote. Its chances improve sharply around a presidential transition, when a new Congress actually has end-of-term rules to strike; otherwise it may sit on the calendar like most non-controversial-seeming procedural bills that never get floor time.
